## Open

### F-362 — the per-namespace Service targeted the gateway port instead of the RPC port

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The first generated Service for an orchestrator namespace published 8080 with targetPort
http-jsonrpc. Namespaces are served by RpcServer and discovered by GatewayCodec as `rpc-<namespace>`
through IResolution, so the Service has to publish the RPC port, 8091 by default, and the resolver
has to strip the rpc- prefix. The wrong port was found only by reading
GatewayCodec.\_discoverService and RpcServer registration; no doc states it. Recorded so a later
manifest change does not reintroduce it.

### F-363 — an adapter namespace was emitted as a Kubernetes Service

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

blong-kustomize derived a Service for every port that declared a namespace, so adding the realm
Kubernetes adapter produced a Service named cluster for a handler group nothing dials. Only a
dispatch orchestrator owns a namespace another process calls; an adapter is local. The planner now
requires port.config.type to be dispatch. Found by regenerating after adding adapter/cluster.ts,
which moved the service count from 1 to 2.

### F-364 — a one-shot prefetch as the only DaemonSet container crash-loops forever

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The nodeLocal backend generated a DaemonSet whose only container fetched and unpacked the artifact.
The fetch succeeded, the container exited 0, and the DaemonSet restarted it immediately:
CrashLoopBackOff with no logs at all, which reads like a broken command rather than a completed one.
A DaemonSet restarts any container that exits, so the fetch is now an init container and the main
container is a placeholder that keeps the pod and its hostPath on the node. Found by applying the
generated tree to the real 2-node cluster.

### F-365 — An adapter that registers only exec answers any prefix-matching method name

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/k8s.ts registers one handler, exec, and reads the middle word of
the triple it is called with to pick an API and a method. Tracing how clusterDeploymentFind reaches
it took several reads: AdapterBase.handle falls back to imported.exec, and handlerProxy resolves any
name the port handles, where handles() is a prefix match against the namespace list. The convention
is provable from test/blong-int-adapter/k8s/test/test/testK8sPodLog.ts, which calls clusterPodFind
and clusterPodLog. Start there next time: one grep for a working call site beats reading the
runtime.

### F-367 — The portal gates every page behind a login the realm does not have

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Running the rewritten Playwright spec failed after 5s waiting for .blong-portal-menubar, and the
failure snapshot showed the app fully up with a login form as its first paint. The portal renders
nothing behind that form, so a realm that loads no login realm cannot reach any page in a browser
run, and D-363 removed login and access with the reason that they need a database. Checking the
premise: realm/blong-login has no adapter/db and no meta folder, and realm/blong-access-mock
substitutes the access realm with hard-coded credentials, so the pair needs no database at all.
Lesson: when a page is unreachable, read the page snapshot in the Playwright error context before
assuming the page code is wrong.

### F-377 — kubectl exec truncates a large stdin stream, kubectl cp does not

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Publishing a 1.2 GB suite archive with kubectl exec -i -- sh -c "cat > file" < /tmp/suite.zip wrote
192 KB and exited cleanly, so the artifact server served a truncated zip and the prefetch unpacked
half a suite with no error of its own. kubectl cp moved the same file in seconds and the size
matched byte for byte. For anything large, copy with kubectl cp and check the size on the far side
before believing the upload, because a short stream is indistinguishable from a successful one by
exit code alone.

### F-381 — A list answer without kind made every live object obsolete

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The reconcile compared desired objects against live ones by kind, namespace and name, and the live
side arrived with only metadata, spec and status, so every key began with a question mark and
nothing matched: the pass reported eighteen creations beside eighteen obsolete objects of the same
kinds, which reads like a broken diff and is really a missing field. The fix was one line once the
probe printed the object's own keys, and the probe would have answered it on the first run; add the
keys to the diagnostic before reading the diff code again (T-226, T-228).

### F-384 — The generate command wrote a second tree under the working directory

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The pattern doc said to run blong ./suite/blong-suite/index.ts k8s from the repository root, and the
default outputDir is a relative path, so the run wrote a whole tree at the repository root beside
the suite real one. The doc now changes into the suite first and the stray tree was removed; a
relative outputDir nobody pins is the trap, and it is silent because both trees look correct.

### F-387 — describe() reports framework components as realms

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The plan for blong-suite carried a deployment named codec, and there is no such realm or package:
the loader creates a component named codec for every process (the protocol layer under
core/blong-gogo/src/codec), and registry describe reports that component as a realm, so the planner
read infrastructure as a business realm and gave it a process and a Service. blong is the same
shape, a component whose realm is the reference realm package. The lesson is that describe().realms
is the set of loaded modules, not the set of business domains, so anything derived per realm has to
classify what it finds rather than trust the list; the role model is that classification.

### F-388 — A static role name left its binding pointing at nothing

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Making the auth-review ClusterRole a cluster constant renamed it to auth-review, but the
ClusterRoleBinding that binds it kept naming the suite-prefixed role, so the pair pointed at a role
that did not exist. Nothing failed loudly: the tree was valid YAML, a test only looked for a file
ending in -role.yaml, and the mistake was found by reading the generated binding while making an
unrelated naming change. The lesson is that a name and every reference to it are one edit, not two,
and that a generated tree makes that cheap to miss because no compiler sees the string. Worth a test
that resolves every roleRef in a tree against the roles it declares.

### F-389 — A grep for a path name missed the source that composes it

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Looking for what reads rc files, I grepped for blongrc and releaserc and concluded nothing in the
framework read one, when blong-config has always called rc with a composed name, blong plus the
intent suffix and blong plus the suite plus the suffix. The names never appear as literals, so the
grep could not see them, and the wrong conclusion went into the plan as a landed note before it was
corrected. Two things would have caught it sooner: reading the config package itself, which is small
and is where the answer was, and treating a grep that returns nothing as weak evidence when the
thing being searched for is a name that has to be built at runtime. The correction cost one honest
sentence in the plan and one question from the user.

### F-390 — A third rc source was added for a name the suffix already produced

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Implementing the release rc pair, the first working version pushed an extra rc call named
blong*releaser. It looked right and did nothing: rc appends rc to whatever name it is given, so that
name resolves to blong_releaserrc, while the mounted path blong_releaserc is already read by the
line that was there all along, rc with blong* plus the trailing intent. The test passed for the
wrong reason, because the existing line supplied the value, which is the kind of evidence that makes
a redundant implementation look verified. The user spotted the extra logic in review. What would
have caught it sooner is asking what the name maps to before adding it — the library is ten lines
and its candidate list is the whole answer — and preferring the convention over a new source, since
an existing mechanism that already produces the required path is the strongest signal that nothing
new is needed.

### F-391 — The bundle path was assumed and was wrong

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Writing the deployment UI's static root, I used the path the plan describes,
/opt/deploy/suite/browser/dist. The real one is /opt/deploy/suite/suite/blong-suite/dist: the
artifact root is the mount, a deploy mirrors the repository's category folders, the suite package
therefore sits at suite/blong-suite inside it, and a suite's own build is vite build, which emits
dist beside the entry. The mistaken path would have been harmless in the way that matters least and
misleading in the way that matters most: the static plugin tolerates a missing root, so a released
suite would have served no page and reported only a warning while the configuration looked
deliberate. The entry path was already written three lines above the line I added, which is the
lesson: the artifact's shape was documented in the very file being edited, and reading it would have
answered the question the plan's prose got wrong.

### F-393 — A new required plan field surfaces as a runtime failure in cast fixtures

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Making portals a required field of IDeploymentPlan broke four tree tests with TypeError plan.portals
is not iterable rather than with a compile error, because those fixtures build a plan literal and
cast it with as never, so the compiler had nothing to check. The lesson is not to avoid the cast,
which is what keeps a fixture readable, but to expect a plan shape change to be a runtime discovery:
the suite names the tests and the field, so the fix is mechanical, and a grep for the old field name
across the realm plus the suite config is what finds the sites before the run does. A second, larger
lesson came with it: the ui field gated two objects and not one, so a suite that declared no ui had
no gateway Service at all and not merely no Ingress, which is why the item looked like a
configuration question and was half a generator one.

### F-394 — A CLI entry point imported by a loaded module deadlocks its own load

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The realm CLI ended in Node's unsettled top-level await warning and no output, and the diagnosis
recorded last time was wrong: it blamed orchestrator/layer.server.ts gating its layer to the k8s
intent, while that file says default true and loads in every intent. The real cause is a module
cycle. The loader imports every module under a layer folder on every load, cli included, because
recording handler folders is what Registry.describe reads; one of the realm's test groups imported
the CLI entry itself to test its command mapping; the entry is mid-evaluation because its own
top-level await runKustomize is what started the load; so the loader awaited a module that awaited
the loader. Node reports that as an unsettled top-level await and exits 13 with nothing printed,
which reads exactly like a hang and is why two probes were needed to find it. The probe that settled
it: the same runKustomize call deferred by one setImmediate works, because by then the entry module
has finished evaluating; the same call from a probe module works for the same reason; and kukum's
CLI works for contrast because nothing in that package imports its bin. The fix is to keep
everything worth testing in a module beside the entry (bin/kustomizeCommand.ts) so the entry has no
inbound import, and the trap is worth knowing because the framework advertises importing a bin from
a test as supported.

### F-395 — A camel-cased call name silently becomes a different method

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The volume prune handler asked the handler proxy for clusterPersistentVolumeClaimFind, which reads
correctly and dispatches nothing of the sort: a method name has exactly three parts, so the proxy
splits what it is handed on the capital letters and sent cluster.persistent.volumeClaimFind to the
adapter, whose middle part is now persistent and which answered no verb matched for
cluster.persistent.volumeClaimFind. The framework's own note in k8s.ts says the adapter answers
resource plus verb, and the realm's testClusterApply spells every compound kind as one word
(clusterPersistentvolumeclaimFind), so the right spelling was already in the package - in a test
file, about a kind nothing else called. What made it expensive is the shape of the failure: the
first run reported that the adapter is not loaded, because a missing proxy method looks like an
absent adapter, and only the run after that surfaced the adapter's own complaint. Both were one
command away, but nothing had run the handler since it was written, which is exactly what T-245
recorded and why the CLI was worth building before anything else on this list.

### F-396 — One deployment walked the deploy path and found six defects

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The user asked for a test deployment of the latest changes on the dev cluster, and walking the whole
path once was worth more than any of the individual fixes in this session. In the order the run met
them: the operator's install tree fetched curl -fsSL empty because operator-entry.ts nested
suiteVolume inside suite, where the plan config does not declare it (the volume is a sibling), so
the realm's own artifact URL was dropped without a word; the suite's CR was written and never
applied because the root kustomization listed folders only, while the comment beside that code
claimed a root document is listed directly; the deployed processes ran microservice alone, so the
portal answered 404 and the two rc files the tree mounts were never the ones the loader read,
because the release block is what names them and what carries the static root; the operator dialled
rpc-cluster for its own adapter, because canSkipSocket is set by the framework for a browser and an
integration run and a deployed process is a third case; and the generation child inherited
BLONG*CONTROLLER*\* from the operator pod, so a k8s run started a nested reconcile loop, failed on a
cluster-wide watch, and took the operator process down with it. Each of those is invisible from the
source: every file involved reads correctly, and only the cluster said otherwise. The lesson is the
one this realm keeps teaching (F-360, F-376): a deployment test is not a smoke test, it is the only
reader that checks the assumptions the code makes about its own environment.

### F-397 — An object method's arrow body is a parse error wearing a type's clothes

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Writing a handler method inside the returned object literal with an arrow body is a syntax error: a
method's body is always a block, so the arrow is where TypeScript stops, and it stops in a way that
reads as a type problem. For the method kustomizeGatewayKeysEnsure tsc reported TS1005 expected
curly plus TS1136 property assignment expected on the return type's own line, which sent me
bisecting the type instead of the body through several probe files; the neighbouring handlers that
parse are the ones whose methods use a block body. The package's tsconfig also sets jsx react, so
the same file reported an eslint Parsing error too, which made the type look guilty twice. The
lesson is to compare a failing signature with a neighbouring one character by character before
theorising: a single grep for the arrow body in the layer showed the only file with it was mine.

### F-399 — A JSON-patch path one level too shallow replaces the whole member

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Rehearsing the CI job's notify step against the dev cluster showed the release patching
/spec/suiteVolume where it meant /spec/suiteVolume/artifact. In JSON patch an add on a member that
exists replaces it, so the operation worked, the answer said updated true, and the suite's volume
lost backend and retention — the CRD's defaults filled the gap, which means a node-local suite
silently became auto because a release happened. Nothing failed and no log line mentioned it; the
only reason it was seen is that the harness printed the CR's spec before and after, which is the
habit worth keeping: a patch's success says nothing about what it replaced, so an assertion belongs
on the _other_ fields. The fix is the nested path, and the paths are now built by an exported
function with a test of its own, because a path is the kind of contract a reading accepts and a test
does not. Found by wiring the pipeline (T-247) rather than by reading it — the same lesson this
realm keeps teaching about deployment runs.

### F-400 — A comment can trip a static scan

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The semantic-log package guards its emit path with a text scan: any shipping module whose source
matches node:net|http|https|dns|tls|dgram|http2 or the word fetch followed by an opening parenthesis
is treated as network code and must be in a declared allowlist. A comment I added explaining that a
payload reference is not something a reader of a release's stdout was meant to fetch, written with a
parenthetical, failed the guard for a module that has no network call at all — the scan reads the
file, not its syntax tree, which is deliberate (it fails the moment such a call is written) and is
why the wording of a comment is part of the contract. The lesson is cheap and reusable: in a package
with an import-graph guard, keep the guarded words out of prose as well as code, and if a scan fails
on a file you only edited comments in, read its regex before reading the file.

### F-403 — A local reconcile with apply wrote junk into the live namespace

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

To see why an apply was failing, the realm CLI was run from the repository as 'bin/kustomize.ts
reconcile --apply --name=blong-suite --namespace=blong-suite'. The from option defaults to registry,
so the pass planned from that process's registry - the realm alone, with no suite around it - and
its deployments are named after the realm's own ports (blong, codec, kustomize). It created three
Deployments and a Service in the live blong-suite namespace, and they had to be deleted by hand. A
registry pass is only meaningful inside the suite's own process; a CR pass needs --from=cr. The
realm could refuse a registry pass whose plan does not match the namespace it is applying into,
which would have said so instead of deploying nonsense.

### F-404 — A stale CR shaped the tree, and the realm believed it

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

externalServices changed from a list to a map keyed by the name the suite resolves. A CR created
before the change kept the old shape, and an apply of the new one across the type change left the
live object holding a list with an empty object in it. The plan then read Object.entries of that
list, produced an entry named 0 with no externalName, and the generator wrote
external-services/0.yaml - an ExternalName Service that addresses nothing. The apply failed with
'Missing key value for ?key?', the reconcile reported one failed step, and the message named neither
the field nor the CR; the only way to see it was to generate the same tree locally from the CR's
spec. Fixed by resolving the declaration through resolveExternalServices, which refuses a list, a
nameless entry and an entry with no externalName, so the failure now names the field. What is still
open is the migration: a CR whose shape changed needs a story, because kubectl apply will not tell
anyone.

### F-407 — The artifact's readiness marker was written before the artifact was whole

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

artifactReady looked for create-links.js in the cache directory, and the fetch command was curl,
unzip, then run that script. The file is not a marker at all: it is a root entry of the archive, and
unzip writes in archive order, so it appears early - measured, the directory held create-links.js
and extractor-metadata.json while suite/ was still absent. A pass that arrived in that window
treated a half-unpacked artifact as ready and handed its entry to the child, which answered 'No
entry point found in /cache/blong-suite/1.13.0'. Two things were wrong at once: the marker was not
written by the step it was standing for, and two passes could fetch into one directory concurrently,
which is how the window opened (a watch pass and the interval behind it both saw an absent
artifact). Fixed with a marker of our own that the fetch removes first and touches last, and an
in-process map that makes a second caller wait for the first fetch instead of starting its own.
Lesson: a marker has to be written by the operation it marks, and 'is it there' is not 'is it
finished'.

### F-416 — The operator regenerated the tree and applied nothing

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Clearing the caches made the operator regenerate the tenant tree with the corrected command line —
the file on disk was blong-suite-migrate-1.13.0-16eec6e1.yaml — yet the pass reported 0 to create, 0
to update and 14 unchanged, so the cluster kept three stale attempts and a first deployment would
have run the Job that cannot work. The current attempt appeared only after the stale Jobs were
deleted by hand, while the same pass printed 4 obsolete and 0 deleted: it knows they are stale
without removing them. Whatever it compares against, it is not the tree it just wrote.

### F-418 — A realm's own config block must sit inside default, not beside it

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

D-433 moved a realm's k8sRealmRole out of the suite and into the realm's own server.ts, and the
first version wrote the block beside default rather than inside it. A realm's config keys are intent
names, so a sibling block is merged only while that intent is active, and the operator runs release
— the declaration would have been invisible in exactly the process that reads it, with no error and
no warning. The answer belongs under default because it is the same in every intent. Second lesson
from the same edit: the planner has to read the nested k8s block of the recorded config rather than
a flat k8sRealmRole, and ??= on a cast whose property is optional is a tsc error — the left-hand
side of an assignment expression may not be an optional property access — so cast to a required
property and coalesce from a non-optional object.

### F-419 — Regenerating a tree by hand loses the flags the e2e script passes

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Regenerating either tree outside scripts/k3d-e2e.sh changes more than the edit: the operator tree
reverted suite.frameworkImage to the published ghcr image, so the new operator pod went
ImagePullBackOff on a cluster whose image is imported as docker.io/library/blong-gogo:1, and passing
an empty artifact URL wrote curl -fsSL with no argument into the cache init container, which is
F-396 exactly. The install tree's default outputDir is relative to the process working directory,
which is why a run from the repository root writes a system/kustomize tree there and leaves the
intended one stale. Regenerate the operator tree with the flags the script uses: outputDir,
suite.frameworkImage, suite.minFrameworkVersion, and the artifact URL only when it is non-empty.

### F-420 — Rebuild the image after a framework change

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The publish cycle has an ordering rule that looks like a formality and is not: a framework change
has to be in the image and in the artifacts before the workloads restart. Here the image was rebuilt
first, the registry fix landed after it, and the artifacts were republished while the image stayed
at the earlier build, so the operator kept planning with the old loader and reported the wrong tree
as unchanged. The generous check is to compare the running pod image id with the digest the build
printed and to grep the published artifact for the changed line, rather than trusting the order of
the steps.

### F-422 — BLONG_ENV carried the namespace, so no deployed pod read an rc file

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Two cluster cycles went into a warning that looked like a mount problem: the file was in the pod and
rc reads exactly that path, but the generated Deployment set BLONG_ENV to the suite namespace and
blong-config prefers BLONG_ENV over the intents it is handed, so the rc app-name became blong suite
rather than blong release and no rc file a deployment mounts was ever read. The lesson: when a file
a deployment mounts has no effect, print the name the reader looks for, not only the path. It also
means the release rc files the generator already mounted predate this change and never worked in a
deployment.

### F-434 — A fixture library cannot call its own builders, and an interface is not a Record

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Two mistakes in the new fixture file, both caught by the type checker and neither by the reader. A
builder written as a property of the object a `library()` returns cannot call a sibling property,
because the properties of an object literal are not in scope inside it: `installPlan` answered with
`suitePlan(...)` and the name did not resolve, so the builders became module-level `const`s and the
library returns them. And a helper typed `Record<string, unknown>` cannot be handed an
`IDeploymentPlan`, because an interface has no index signature: the parameter is typed `object`,
which is what a plan is assignable to. The second one is the trap worth remembering, since the same
signature is what a configuration merge helper naturally wants.

### F-436 — A merge patch cannot remove a key, so a probe left a path on a live CR

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

scripts/reconcile-local.sh patched the CR artifact to a local path and restored it with a merge
patch carrying the saved value; merging source: url back over source: path left the path behind, so
the CR named a laptop directory while it also named the artifact URL. The restore now replaces the
field with a json patch, and removes it when the CR carried none. Lesson: restoring a field a probe
invented must be a replacement, never a merge, or the field it added survives the restore.

### F-439 — A rebuilt image under the same tag never reaches a pod that already exists

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The framework image is imported into the k3d nodes under a fixed tag
(docker.io/library/blong-gogo:1), and a pod that already exists keeps running whatever that tag
resolved to when it started: an unchanged spec makes `kubectl apply -k` a no-op, so the Deployment
is not rolled, and a container restart reuses the image id recorded in the pod's status instead of
re-resolving the tag. An operator stuck in a crash loop therefore stays on exactly the code that put
it there, even after the build and the import have replaced the image on that node, which is how a
cycle that had already published the fix sat on "Waiting for deployment blong-operator rollout to
finish: 0 of 1 updated replicas are available" until the rollout status check before REFRESH timed
out after 300s and failed the run — before the REFRESH step that would have restarted the pod could
be reached, leaving the tenant processes on an artifact that still had the ENOTFOUND the fix was
for. Deleting the pod is what resolves it
(`kubectl -n blong-system delete pod -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=blong-operator`, whose label
selector also takes the cache DaemonSet pods, which are recreated by their own controller), and the
lesson is that every publish step needs a restart of whatever already runs what was published. F-420
records the ordering half of the same trap.

### F-440 — A kustomization namespace field rewrites every object in the tree

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The suite root kustomization carried `namespace: blong-suite`, and that field is not a default for
objects that forgot one but a rewrite: kustomize sets `metadata.namespace` on every namespace-able
object, overwriting whatever the object declared, and renames every Namespace object in the tree to
it. A tree that carries a second namespace therefore cannot keep the field at all — adding the
services namespace made the build die with `namespace transformation produces ID conflict` because
`blong-services` was renamed onto the suite's own Namespace, and had the two not collided the
generated workload would have been pulled back into the suite's namespace, which is the failure the
feature exists to avoid. No annotation opts out (`kustomize.config.k8s.io/behavior: none` changed
nothing), which was worth testing against the binary rather than trusting to memory. The lesson: the
field belongs in a kustomization only while the tree holds one namespace, and a tree that grows a
second one says so per document — including the folders whose objects are built by a generator (the
secrets and assets folders), which carry no namespace of their own and therefore need theirs named
in the folder kustomization so removing the root field does not move them into whatever namespace
the caller applies from.

### F-441 — A pod is Running while its container is in a crash loop

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The e2e picked its probe pod with `--field-selector=status.phase=Running`, and a pod whose container
keeps crashing satisfies that: its phase is Running because the pod is scheduled and its container
is being restarted, while `kubectl exec` answers
`unable to upgrade connection: container not found`. The guard that follows a `kubectl exec` failure
is an `if`, so the dial the section exists to make was skipped with a printed note on exactly the
cluster that needed it — a check that fails open, which is worse than no check. Selected by
container readiness instead:
`-o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,READY:.status.containerStatuses[*].ready'` and an awk that
keeps the first row whose READY is true. The general shape is worth remembering for any e2e that
wants a process to talk to: readiness is a property of the container, and phase is not it.

### F-443 — A base's header comment was read as a use of a placeholder

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Every base opens by listing the placeholders a base may use, and the renderer substitutes over the
whole file text — so the header of a base for a service with no credentials asked for
${credentialsSecret}, which that service has no value for, and the generation of a file that would
have applied failed with an error naming a comment. The new step that renders every descriptor with
its own base is what found it: the six bases written in one sitting were all correct as documents
and one was wrong as a template, which is exactly the class of mistake a header cannot check for
itself. Fixed by substituting per line and skipping the ones that open with a comment, because a
header should describe what a base may say rather than depend on it — the same reasoning as the
placeholder list itself, which exists so a base names nothing the plan decides.

### F-445 — Three shell-runbook defects that only a rewrite could show

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Rewriting the k3d runbook in TypeScript exposed three faults the bash version had carried without
ever reporting them. A resource and its name passed as one argv entry means kubectl is asked for a
type called 'ingress shop-test', so a jsonpath read answers empty and an assertion reads a missing
host rather than a wrong call — the shell hid it because a command substitution that fails is also
empty. A spawned tool started with --target=URL rather than --target URL reads the value as nothing
and answers on its own default port, which looks like a timeout. And a background tool whose stderr
is sent to /dev/null leaves a wait that times out with no reason at all; keeping the last lines and
printing them turns a mystery into one line.

### F-447 — A handler needs a port namespace to be callable

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

A layer folder is discovered and its handlers are attached, but a method is only reachable through a
port that names a namespace: without one the framework answers 'unknown method' while the handlers
sit registered and inert, and nothing says which of the two is missing. The tap groups are a
different path — they are read straight from server/test/test/ — so the assertions passed for an
hour while every command failed, which is the evidence that sent the search the wrong way. Two more
facts from the same hour: a custom top-level folder is not discovered at all (the deployment realm
says so in its own server.ts, and its answer is to keep the steps in orchestrator/), and a custom
layer needs the cli intent's layers named in the component config because cli appears in no entry of
the well-known layer table, plus a logLevel for the intent or the dispatch events land in the middle
of the command's stdout.

### F-448 — A one-shot migration step ran while the artifact volume was being replaced

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The prefetch DaemonSet replaces the suite volume in place — it removes the marker, wipes the
directory and unpacks the archive — so a pod scheduled in the same moment reads a half-written tree.
Nothing in the generated tree waited for the marker, and the migration Job has one attempt
(`backoffLimit: 0`), so it died on ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for a module that unzip had not reached yet,
while the same file was in the archive, in the local install and in the volume a minute later. Two
costs: the failure reads like a broken package rather than a race, and it only appears when the
volume is being filled or refilled, which a long-lived cluster hides until a run happens to lose.

### F-450 — A re-applied fill Job is refused once its template moves

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

kubectl apply of the operator tree failed on the two fill Jobs with
`spec.template: field is immutable` after the generator changed their pod spec, because a Job's
template cannot be patched. In steady state this is invisible: the Job's name carries the artifact
identity, so a new artifact is a new Job and the old one is pruned by retention. It bites only a
developer who regenerates a tree for an artifact the cluster already filled, where the remedy is to
delete the completed fill Job first. Worth knowing before reading the error as a broken tree.

### F-451 — A realm change is only in the cluster once the artifact is rebuilt

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

After the generator gained the second mount, a full cycle run went green and every workload rolled
out, which looked like proof that the fix worked. It was not: the reconciled suite Deployments still
mounted the old version-only path with no second mount, and the pods only stayed healthy because
that stale host directory is a self-consistent tree left by the previous in-place fill, whose links
point at /opt/deploy/suite and resolve. Two facts combine. A tree the CLI applies is overwritten
within a minute by the operator's reconcile, because the operator owns those Deployments (spec-hash
label). And the operator renders them in a short-lived child that loads the _tenant's artifact_ — so
it runs the realm code in the published zip, not the repository. With BUILD_SUITE=0 the zip is not
rebuilt, so the child kept rendering the old tree and the cluster validated code nobody had changed.
The lesson is that a cluster check on this realm is only about the published artifact: rebuild and
publish it, or read the generated tree the operator holds
(`/cache/generations/<suite>/deployments/<name>.yaml`, beside the CR spec in `<suite>-spec.json`)
and see which identity and which mounts the applied tree actually carries.

### F-453 — A patched list element moves to the front of its list

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The instantiated overlay composed to the flat tree everywhere except one thing: the fill container's
environment, where the identity came back first instead of second. Kustomize's strategic merge does
not replace a list element in place — the element a patch names is placed at the front of the list,
in the patch's order, with the patch's own entries leading. So a patch that names one entry of a
list reorders it, which is invisible to Kubernetes (env order means nothing) and visible to anyone
diffing two trees, which is how it was found: the acceptance check is a byte comparison of kubectl
kustomize output against the flat tree, and it caught a twelve-line difference. The fix is to have a
patch carry the whole list it touches (the fill environment does), or to patch the entry the
generator writes first (the suite volume, which every workload writes first) — and to keep the byte
comparison, because it is the only thing that sees this class of difference.

### F-398 — A lookup that matches nothing reads as a timeout

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The CR-driven pass reported one failed step for forty minutes and the message was the step did not
finish within 300s, which sent the reading towards the Job and the API server: both Jobs were
Complete, so the obvious next question was what the API was answering. It was answering nothing. The
wait looks a Job up by labelSelector on the name label and the object's own name, and that label
carries the suite on every generated object while the object's own name is on the instance label, so
the selector matched no object at all and the loop polled an empty list until the deadline. The
message could not say so, and that is the defect worth remembering: a timeout reported without what
it looked for and what it saw is indistinguishable from a slow cluster, and the reader goes and
checks the cluster instead of the selector. Two changes came out of it: the lookup uses the instance
label, and the timeout now reports how many objects the lookup answered. The probe that settled it
was a local pass on the CLI (reconcile --from=cr) printing the failure array with its message,
because the operator's own log records the counts and the status records only the first key. Getting
that probe to run found a second defect on the way: the tree generation child re-runs
`process.argv[1]`, which for the realm CLI is the CLI itself, so it answered with the realm's usage
text.

### F-468 — A namespace-scoped listing made a healthy suite look broken

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The failure was named after the wrong half of the pass. The CR said
`Failed ... first: PersistentVolumeClaim/blong-services/mysql-data` while every workload of the
suite was `Available`, and the operator log showed a 422 on the claim's _replace_ — a PUT, which a
bound claim refuses — because the pass had decided that claim was `to create` on every pass: it
listed live objects in the tenant's namespace only, so the suite's five objects in the services
namespace (workload, claim, Service, init ConfigMap, credentials Secret) were invisible to it, and
applying an object that already exists is a PUT. Two things made it findable and both are worth
keeping: the cluster-state dump the job collects puts the CR status next to the workloads, and the
status counts were the tell — `mysql available: 0` reported beside a mysql Deployment that was 1/1
Available can only come from reading the wrong namespace. The lesson: when a pass wants to create an
object that plainly exists in the cluster, suspect the scope of its listing before its apply path,
and read the counts it writes about itself as claims about where it looked.

### F-461 — A drop that deletes a namespace takes the rights with it

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The dev script's DROP_SERVICES deletes the blong-services namespace so a switched-off service does
not sit in the cluster, and the namespace holds the operator's tenant Role and RoleBinding as well
as the service. The operator may not re-create them, because the RBAC kinds are install-owned by
design, so after the first drop every pass failed to read the leftovers there, the CR stayed Failed,
and the next cycle's wait for Ready timed out — the script reported a failure with a message about a
step in a namespace that looked empty. A destructive convenience that removes a namespace owns
everything in it, including the RBAC somebody else granted; either re-apply what the drop took or
delete by kind and leave the grants.

A listing that fails is now reported as a step of its own — the failure names the namespace and the
kind — rather than ending the pass before it writes a status (D-499), so this state is readable from
the CR instead of only from the operator log.

### F-472 — The reconcile diff was described from its caller, not its code

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

T-318 asserted that the reconcile's diff compares the desired object with the live one whole, and
that a server-owned `volumeName` therefore read as a change on every pass. The diff does no such
thing: `diffResources` compares the `spec-hash` label the tree stamps on each manifest with the
label the apply wrote onto the live object — plan against plan, not object against object, which is
exactly why a field the server owns cannot affect it. The claim came from the numbers beside it
(`updated: 1` for a tree nobody had edited) and from the call site in the reconcile, rather than
from reading `diffResources` and `stampSpecHash`, which would have taken one file open and would
have shown the permanent update for what it was: the failed apply never writing the new label. The
lesson is the one this repository keeps teaching — read the function before describing its
behaviour, and treat a count as evidence to explain rather than as proof of a mechanism.

### F-475 — The split's third half was missing from two of its readers

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Two wires were missing from the split's third half, and no test could see either. The pass applies
what `kustomizeSuiteGenerate` composes, and that composed `base` + `local` only, so an opted-in
service's objects were absent from the tree the pass reconciles: it never applied them and read
every live one as obsolete, which would have pruned the alias and the credentials copy the runbook
had just written, and the switch-off assertions would have passed for the wrong reason. Merging the
folders in exposed the second: the overlay's own objects were missing too - the namespace a service
runs in and the operator's rights there, which D-504 moved out of the base - so the composed set was
still two ids short. Both were found by adding a service to the plan in the materialization test;
every existing test used a plan with no service. The lesson is that a layout with three halves has
three readers (kustomize, the JavaScript materializer the pass applies, and the composition the test
checks), and a change to the halves has to be made in all of them.

### F-476 — Three kustomize constraints found by composing the overlay

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Composing the two-level overlay taught three kustomize constraints, each of which cost a rewrite
cycle and none of which is stated where the generator looks. A parent kustomization's `namespace:`
field is applied after its children are built, so it rewrites the namespace a child declared: a
field on the overlay's root pulls a service folder's workload into the tenant's namespace, which is
what forced the overlay to become a namespace-free root with two namespace-declaring children. Two
objects of one kind and name in one kustomization are one resource id and are refused
(`may not add resource with an already registered id`) — which is what stripping the namespace
exposed, because the alias collided with the workload's own Service and the credentials copy with
the workload's Secret, both differing only by namespace. Moving each into the suite's child fixed
it, because a child's namespace transformer runs during its own build. And a patch must live below
the directory of the kustomization that names it (`security; file … is not in or below …`), so the
overlay's patches and instances both moved under `local/suite/`. The lesson is to compose a minimal
two-namespace tree with `kubectl kustomize` before writing the tree that needs it, rather than
reasoning about the semantics.

### F-477 — A skip guard turned a missing requirement into a green run

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Two composition steps were written with a
`try { execFileSync('kubectl', …) } catch { return {skipped: …} }` guard, and the guard was the
defect rather than the safety net. A step that reports a skip when its dependency is missing turns a
missing requirement into a green run: the report says the group passed, the half of the contract
that only that binary checks was never exercised, and nothing distinguishes it from a run that did
check it. The crux is that a guard belongs around a _choice_ — the repo's own `BLONG_TEST_APPLY=1`
gate, where skipping is the point — and not around a _requirement_, whose absence is a failure the
message has to name. The test is whether the machine can reasonably be expected to have the
dependency: `kubectl` is on a developer's machine and on the CI runner, so its absence is a broken
environment rather than an unsupported one. The mistake is easy to repeat because a skip reads as
defensive coding.

### F-484 — A folded YAML scalar flattens a generated program

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

A multi-line string in a ConfigMap data value is written as a folded block scalar, so its line
breaks become spaces and it is re-wrapped at the width. A three-hundred-line program arrives that
way and does not parse, and because kustomize re-emits the value it parsed, the flattening survives
into the cluster. The fill module travels as binaryData instead: base64 is one line, no style folds
it, and the kubelet decodes it back into the bytes the realm wrote. The companion trap is that the
split-versus-flat comparison failed on the label set alone: every object the generator writes
carries the suite labels itself, so an object built by a helper that forgot them differs from its
composed counterpart in nothing else and the identity map both sides are keyed by still matched.

### F-489 — The operator serves the page, but the portal cannot render it

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The last mile works and the page stops one call short. Giving the realm a real build script (it was
literally true, so there was no bundle), naming that bundle as a static root in the operator's
release block, and running a cycle put the page on the operator's gateway: the browser gets
index.html and the module graph, the portal logs in with a service-account token, and the menubar
renders — the screenshot shows Blong Kustomize, the Kustomize menu item and the profile menu. What
stays empty is the content area, because the portal asks the same gateway for the model schema and
gets 401 (missing authorization header, from the bearer hook in jwt.ts) and then 500 (TypeError
fetch failed, with no host named). So the operator answers a call the page needs by reaching for
something it does not serve, and the page fails silently rather than showing an error. Driving the
deployed page with Playwright is what found it: curl sees a healthy page and no unit test asks a
browser to render one.

### F-491 — A framework realm is shipped and resolvable but its orchestrator never activates

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

After the page's missing method was traced to the framework realm, everything about shipping it was
verified: blong-server is a declared dependency of the realm, it travels in the operator's artifact
(core/blong-server, linked into realm/blong-kustomize/node_modules), it imports inside the pod, and
the pod's own operator-entry.ts is the current one with the srv child and both selectors on its
command line. It still does not activate: the deployed process logs no server.subject at all, while
the realm's own CLI logs server.subject with the identical config key. So the two mechanisms
available for turning a layer on for a process do not reach this realm when it is attached by the
framework: a parent config key (server: {orchestrator: true}) works for the realm CLI and not for
the operator, and the command-line selector (--server.orchestrator) has no visible effect in the pod
either. What the next reader should look at is the activation path in core/blong-gogo/src/load.ts
for a realm the framework attaches itself (frameworkRealms) under a release intent, with T-238 as
the map: the realm answers to two spellings, and a selector that misses activates nothing and says
nothing.

### F-492 — Activating a realm and denying its adapter must share one name spelling

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

In the operator pod `--srv.orchestrator` does activate the framework realm (the log then shows
`srv.subject` and `srv.db`), but the `--server.adapter=false` passed beside it matched no realm, so
the db adapter dialled host `db` (`Error: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND db`) and every
`/rpc/subject/object/schema` call answered 500, which the page shows only as an empty table. The
loader keeps whichever name a realm loads under (T-238), so an activation selector and the deny that
must undo its side effect have to be spelled the same way — passing both spellings is the form that
works whichever one lands. The same asymmetry makes the realm CLI (which answers to `server`) and
the deployed pod (which answers to `srv`) need different spellings for the identical intent.

### F-496 — The realm test run dies of tap's global timeout

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

node --run test on this realm spends minutes in the cluster groups and hits tap's 240 second global
timeout, which reports the whole run as 'expired: index.test.ts' and turns every group that had not
started into a failure. A run that looked like seven broken tests was one slow run plus the two real
failures inside it. TAP_TIMEOUT raises the bound and the same suite finished in six seconds with the
cluster groups skipping, so read the per-step lines and not only the summary line.

### F-502 — A registry pass that applies hangs on a fill Job it never created

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

A pass with `apply: true` from the registry origin builds its tree before the artifact is
materialized, so the volume identity is empty and the plan names
`blong-operator-fill-0.1.0-k3d-dev-cluster-agent-0` where the cluster holds
`blong-operator-fill-0.1.0-7b132846-k3d-dev-cluster-agent-0`. The apply then waits for that Job
through `waitForStep`, and a Job that was never created never completes, so the pass answers nothing
at all: the page waits 60s for a response that never arrives and a curl times out after 180s. The
same call with `apply: false` answers in 40ms with the same tree, which is what told the two origins
apart. Diagnosing it needed the MLE proxy (`blong-dev proxy`) to call the gateway with plain JSON:
neither the browser nor the operator log says a pass is blocked.

### F-503 — A cycle builds the framework image and never imports it into the nodes

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Five cycles in a row produced a new operator pod in ImagePullBackOff while the same command had
worked before, and two things were wrong together. The image is built and tagged
(`Successfully tagged localhost/blong-gogo:1`) but nothing puts it into the k3d nodes:
`lib/images.ts` owns that step (`podman save`, `podman cp` into each node,
`ctr -n k8s.io images import`) and it did not run, while `k3d image import` cannot do it either
because it insists on the docker daemon this machine does not use. Then the applied Deployment
carried `imagePullPolicy: Always`, so a node that already has the image still tries Docker Hub and
fails, where an earlier pod of the same Deployment was defaulted to IfNotPresent. The workaround
both times was to tag, save, copy into both nodes, import there, and JSON-patch the policy back to
IfNotPresent — with a merge patch refused because a container entry needs its image repeated.
VERIFYING A DELIVERY IS THEREFORE NOT JUST RUNNING THE CYCLE.

### F-506 — A cycle serves the realm dist and never rebuilds it

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The Reconcile test kept failing with a 60s timeout and the operator log showed the registry shape,
so both the action params and the handler looked wrong — neither was. The served bundle was the one
built the previous day: the realm `dist/` is a build output, the cycle builds the _framework image_
and packs the suite artifact, and nothing in that path runs `vite build` for the realm. A
browser-side change therefore looks exactly like a change that was never applied, and the only way
to tell was to read the served chunk out of the running pod (`grep -A 2 method:` under
`/opt/deploy/suite/realm/blong-kustomize/dist/assets`). Running `node --run build` in the realm and
cycling again fixed it at once: the page went from a 60s timeout to RECONCILE 200 in 2.8s.

### F-511 — A comment sweep rewrote the realm's own memory files

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The mechanical conversion walked every tracked file under the realm, including
`.github/memory/*.md`, and rewrote bare ids there into `@@` — wrong, because a memory file's own ids
are meant to stay bare (the CLI owns those files). It was caught by diffing the memory tree and
recovered with git checkout. A whole-tree sweep must exclude the memory tree, and any file whose ids
the CLI owns, before it writes; the sweep script's file filter is the place to put that rule.

### F-513 — A suite entry path must name the folder the artifact carries

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

`rush deploy` mirrors the repository's category folders into the artifact, so the operator's file
sits at realm/blong-kustomize/operator-entry.ts and an entry has to carry that prefix — the same
rule the suite's own entry follows, suite/blong-suite/index.ts inside the suite's mount. Without it
the install tree named /opt/deploy/suite/operator-entry.ts, a file no artifact has. The framework
then fell back to looking in its own working directory and the operator exited with "No entry point
found in /opt/deploy", which names the directory rather than the entry and sends a reader to the
wrong place. The entry is absolute for the reason SUITE_MOUNT gives: a path is absolute inside the
artifact, not inside the container.

### F-517 — A comments-only sweep changed an artefact embedded from source bytes

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The prose sweep trimmed the comments in realm/blong-kustomize/fill.ts and CI failed in the same
package for a reason that had nothing to do with prose: fill.ts is embedded byte for byte into the
fill-script ConfigMap, and two committed artefacts are built from those bytes — the install tree
under system/operator and the tap snapshot of the generated tree, whose spec-hash is a hash of the
module. Nothing regenerated them: the snapshot expected the pre-sweep bytes and the tree still held
them, so a comment-only edit failed a test in a package nobody touched. The class is what matters: a
derived artefact needs a command that regenerates it, and a source that is embedded rather than
imported has to be embedded in a form prose cannot change.

### F-518 — A base ConfigMap applied with -f landed in the context namespace

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

Verifying the minified fill on the k3d cluster took three cycles and the first two proved nothing.
The object a probe pod mounts lives in `blong-system`, but `kubectl apply -f` and
`kubectl replace -f` on the generated `system/operator/base/configmaps/fill-script.yaml` never
changed it: a base file carries no `namespace`, so the update goes to the context namespace
(`blong-suite` here), and the copy the pod read stayed at the module from before the prose sweep.
Both commands print a success line, so the run that followed looked like a pass while the pod was
running the old bytes.

What changed the object was naming it: `kubectl -n blong-system patch cm fill-script --type=merge`
with a `--patch-file` holding the module in `binaryData` and the same label hash the tree carries.
What proved it was fingerprinting the mounted artefact inside the pod rather than trusting the exit
code: print `wc -c` and the first characters of the file, so a stale mount is visible as 19292 bytes
of commented source instead of 6354 bytes of minified code.

Lesson: a generated base is applied with `-k` (which supplies the namespace) or with the namespace
pinned on the command, and a cluster probe asserts on what the container actually mounted, not on
its own success message.

### F-519 — A staged ignored file failed the pre-commit lint gate

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The commit could not be made, twice, and both times the blocker was the same thing: a generated file
that has to be committed. The derived module `fill.min.mts` sits in the package's source tree, so
the staged linter picked it up as source and eslint reported 57 errors against minified output —
`prefer-const` and `no-unused-expressions`, style the minifier will never honour. The package's own
`eslint.config.mjs` now ignores it, using the shape `core/blong-kukum` already uses for its
committed fixture: a global-ignore object first, then the shared config.

Only after that did the second cause show. Naming an ignored file on the eslint command line makes
eslint warn that the file is ignored, and `blong-dev lint` runs eslint with `--max-warnings 0`, so
the warning failed the run: `0 error(s), 1 warning(s)` and a failed package. `core/blong-lint` now
passes `--no-warn-ignored`, which skips such a file exactly as a whole-package run does; real
diagnostics still fail, because the flag only silences that one warning.

Lesson for the next derived artefact: excluding a generated file from the formatter is not enough,
the staged linter has to be told as well, and at zero warnings an ignored-file warning reads as a
lint failure rather than as nothing to check.

What the artefact needed in total: `.prettierignore` for the formatter, the package's eslint config
for the linter, and nothing for tsc, which never sees it because the package include is `**/*.ts`
and `**/*.tsx` and `.mts` matches neither.

### F-563 — The operator crashed on a devDependency imported by a test handler

> _2026-10-17 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The operator CrashLoopBackOff on the kustomize end-to-end run: ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for @swc/core
imported from scripts/minifyFill.ts, at /opt/deploy/suite/realm/blong-kustomize, five restarts deep,
so the CR never reported a phase and wait-operator.sh timed out after five minutes. The cause is
that the loader imports the files of a layer before it decides whether the layer is active: every
process that loads the realm executes server/test/test/testFill.ts, whatever the intent, and that
file imported the minifier at module scope. @swc/core is a devDependency, so rush deploy --scenario
operator leaves it out of the tree. Local runs hid it because the repo has the package installed.
Reproduce without a cluster: rush deploy --scenario operator --target-folder
/tmp/deploy-operator --overwrite, node create-links.js create, then blong /tmp/deploy-operator/
realm/blong-kustomize/operator-entry.ts release; a temporary stub at realm/blong-kustomize/
node_modules/@swc/core that logs its import stack names the importer. Fixed by resolving the
minifier inside the one case that needs it, so the release process never touches it. The realm suite
is 117 passed.

### F-615 — The CR example is the file the runbook applies

> _2026-10-27 · realm/blong-kustomize · open_

The declaration a split ships beside its base is not merely a sample a reader copies:
declarationApply applies example/blongdeployment.yaml, so writing a placeholder into its portal host
— the obvious way to keep a deployment's domain out of a committed file — put host PLACEHOLDER into
the live CR and left the portal certificate on the old issuer with no error anywhere. The real
declaration is now written to local/declaration/blongdeployment.yaml, which is ignored, and the
example stays the sample; a generator change to a committed file that a step reads has to be traced
to that step first.

## Resolved

### F-371 — The browser login fails while the same handler authenticates the token

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The client never sent the request. `authLogin` reported
`remote.bindingFailed: Method binding failed for req request login.token.create`, the trace showed
the MLE session handshake and no `/rpc/login/token.create` after it, and the page showed nothing at
all because `authLogin` returns rather than throws when a response carries no token. The earlier
`invalid bearer token` was a red herring: the form was filling correctly and no credential ever
reached the cluster.

A realm that answers `login.token.create` itself has to register that namespace in the front-end
orchestrator, in `browser/orchestrator/subject/init.ts`, beside its own subject —
`namespace: ['kustomize', 'login']`. The folder name `subject` stays literal: a declaration file
under a folder named after the namespace does not bind, which is where the first attempt went. A
second attempt loaded the port and its handler group on the browser as well, which did bind the call
and then ran the handler in the browser, where the cluster adapter does not exist (the error moved
to `cluster.token_review.create`); both attempts were reverted before the working one.

Two diagnostics stayed, both at warn level, because each failure this cost was a silent one:
`authLogin` warns with the error type and message in the message text — a pino object prints as
`Object`, which is how the reason stayed invisible — and the login handler warns with the refusal
reason and the length of the token it was given, never the token itself, so a truncated credential
cannot pass for an unknown one. Verified: the Playwright spec passes with a fresh service-account
token, and the realm suite is 17 of 17.

### F-374 — A deploy artifact needs a link step and an absolute entry

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

Two things the first live deployment proved about the artifact. Rush deploy writes create-links.js
rather than links, because an archive cannot carry symlinks, so the prefetch has to run it after
unpacking or every import of a realm resolves to nothing: the fetch script now does, which is
generated code. And the runner imports the entry exactly as given, so a relative entry resolves
against blong.ts rather than the working directory and has to be absolute, which is F-360 seen from
inside a container. The image needs the same link step for its own deploy folder.

Both halves are in the tree now. The prefetch fetch step runs the artifact link script after
unpacking, and every entry the generator emits is an absolute path, because the framework imports
the target as written and a relative one resolves against the framework directory; the default entry
was still relative and is now absolute too. The realm snapshot holds the absolute default.

### F-392 — A plausible file read was taken as the diagnosis

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The realm CLI ended in Node's unsettled top-level await warning with no output, and this entry
originally recorded the cause as orchestrator/layer.server.ts gating its layer to the k8s intent,
because the realm's server.ts says so in its opening comment. That comment is stale: the layer file
itself reads default true. The real cause was a module cycle, found only by probing - the loader
imports every module under a layer folder on every load, cli included; one of the realm's test
groups imported the CLI entry; the entry was mid-evaluation at its own top-level await, which is
what started that load. The lesson is about evidence rather than about loaders: a comment that names
a mechanism is a claim, not a reading, and the file it points at is one grep away. The second lesson
is that the first fit between symptom and story is not a diagnosis - the gate theory explained the
silence and was wrong, and only the probe that deferred the call by one setImmediate settled it.

Superseded by the real cause in F-394; the comment in server.ts that misled this reading is now the
thing to fix.

### F-410 — A CRD default that reaches an attempt name splits one step into two

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

A fresh cluster therefore had two migration attempts for one step, the first of which ran before its
node volume was seeded and failed with 'No entry point found in /opt/deploy'. The lesson
generalises: once a CRD declares a default, every hash over the CR fields differs between the
declared file and the live object, so hash resolved values rather than optional inputs.

jobName now hashes the argv alone; the defaults omitted and the defaults spelled out produce one
name, pinned by theAttemptNameIgnoresHowTheIntentsWereSpelled

### F-406 — The attempt's name did not cover the command line the step runs

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

jobName hashes what a deploy-time Job runs, so a changed attempt arrives as a different name and
nothing has to be updated - that is the reason a Job is immutable and the pass leaves an existing
attempt alone. The hash covered the kind, the suite, the version, the image, the minimum framework
version, the entry, the intents and whether the suite has a database, but not the argv those inputs
produce: T-253 moved db in front of the intents and the name d7aca82b did not move with it. The live
cluster therefore held an attempt running the old command line while the tree carried the corrected
one under the same name, and after a Job was made un-updatable the difference was invisible - the
pass reported 15 unchanged and the CR said Ready over a step that no longer matched the tree. Fixed
by extracting migrationArgs and hashing the argv itself. Lesson: a name that stands in for a spec
has to hash the spec, not the inputs the spec is derived from, or a derivation change is a silent
no-op.

The argv is hashed and the intents field no longer is (F-410); confirmed live on dev-cluster where
the tenant tree and the operator name one attempt (1f770a10) and a pass reports 0 to update, waiting
for it rather than replacing an immutable Job

### F-411 — A realm fix needs the suite artifact rebuilt, not only the operator

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The staged copy is the one that produced the name, and the string plan.suite.intents alone proves
nothing because the argv fallback reads it too (three occurrences in the fixed file as well). So a
change to this realm reaches a running cluster only after the suite artifact is republished and the
operator's cached copy of the suite is cleared: the runbook warns about the cache, not about which
of the two copies runs. The name grid that identified the three attempts (a49b82e7 old without
intents, ebc5b94d old with them, 1f770a10 new) is the check that separates code that did not run
from a hash that did not move.

The runbook now names which of the two copies generates a child's tree and why a fresh kustomize.zip
is not enough.

### F-414 — A positional after a --flag is swallowed by the parser

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The migration step's argv put the selectors before the intents, so the trailing release
followed --marine.orchestrator; minimist reads that as the flag's value, the release intent never
reached the config, and the step spent four attempts dialling the adapter's default 127.0.0.1:3306
while every pod beside it connected to db. Every hand-run repro used the other order and connected,
which is what hid it: a positional is only positional when no flag precedes it. The intents are
emitted before the flags now, and the tree generator's own test asserts that no positional follows a
flag.

### F-417 — A route hunt that was really a missing listener

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

T-261 sent the reader into the registration path — the port imports patterns, the registry register
call, the localOnly guard, the route builder in the rpc server — and none of it was the cause: the
operator process runs no gateway at all, and the path the docs name is a gateway route, so every
kustomize route 404s while the tenant answers 401 on a route of the same shape. The measurement that
settles it takes one line and was available from the start: read the listening ports out of the
process log and the Service, then ask which of the two servers owns the documented path. The entry
had already observed 404 and had reasoned about which string a pattern is matched against instead; a
probe of a sibling route would have shown it was not a pattern question at all. Lesson: a 404 whose
body names the server that answers is evidence about the listener, not about the handler.

The listener question is answered and the fix landed; the lesson stays in the body.

### F-425 — Pruning dangling images threw away the build cache and made every build cold

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The first version of the retention line in `k3d-dev-cycle.sh` ran
`podman image prune -f --filter dangling=true` after importing the image. Buildah leaves its stage
images dangling, but they are also the layer cache: the manifest and source copies, `rush install`
and `rush deploy` all live in them, so the next build re-executed everything. The build log showed
four cache hits in a sixty-six step build, with `rush install` (the 3 GB dependency tree plus the
native build of `node-rdkafka`) and `rush deploy` both running from scratch — the ten to fifteen
minutes T-263/F-411 measured, paid on every cycle. Retention has to be per generation rather than
blanket: the epoch is taken before `podman build` and the prune runs with
`--filter until=<elapsed>s`, which drops the superseded generations and leaves the chain just built
standing, so the cache stays warm and disk stays bounded to one generation. Lesson: a dangling image
is not automatically garbage here — on this builder it is the cache, so prune by age relative to the
current run, never by dangling alone.

fixed by pruning by age relative to the build start; the next full cycle reused the cache (58 of 66
steps, install and deploy both cached) and the store fell from 9.281 GB to 8.522 GB with one fresh 4
GB generation kept for the run after it.

### F-430 — The operator portal login has never been reachable in the dev cluster

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The cluster-backed login creates a TokenReview with the operator service account, and the operator
ClusterRole has no rule for it, so every portal login answers `Kubernetes Access Forbidden`. A
temporary ClusterRole proved the handler and the readable separator naming both work — the log leg
is `cluster.token_review.create` and the answer carries the token — which is how the gap was told
apart from a naming failure: a wrong name reaches the adapter error, not the API server. The suite
own login (the blong-login realm) is what the cycle exercises, so nothing noticed.

resolved by the same change; the tree test now asserts the operator's two review rules, so the gap
cannot come back unnoticed.

### F-432 — The generated steps ran BestEffort while the processes were sized

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

Every process a suite serves carried `resources` from the plan default, and every container the
generator emitted around them — the seed and migration Jobs, the node prefetch and the placeholder
that keeps its pod — carried none, so the scheduler treated them as BestEffort and a cluster that
enforces limits would refuse them. Nothing in the tree said so: the migration Job shipped that way
from the day it existed, and it was visible only by reading a running pod. The fix is one helper
beside the plan default, used by every emitted container, and the tree test now walks every pod spec
and fails when one is unsized.

fixed in this change

### F-444 — A prune that only looks up the kinds its tree names

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The pass builds one lookup per resource type from the tree it applies, so a kind that leaves the
tree is never looked up and its objects stay behind. The credentials copy a switched-off service
wrote into the suite namespace is a Secret, and a tree with no Secret left builds no secret group,
which orphaned the copy by the pass that was meant to remove it. The runbook applies its own tree
with kubectl apply -k before the operator converges, so the copy existed on the cluster and looked
like the operator had applied it.

fixed by the sweep in D-464

### F-446 — A forgotten cluster variable becomes a second cluster

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The k3d runbook defaults CLUSTER to blong-e2e while the developer's cluster is dev-cluster, and the
cycle creates the cluster it does not find — so a run that forgot to pass CLUSTER did not fail, it
started building a second cluster beside the running one. That build then stalled with its agent
node and load balancer left in Created and never started, which is a podman stall rather than a k3d
error, and the script waited for it for eighteen minutes with no output to read. Two lessons: the
steps that create infrastructure should refuse to do so unless the caller asks, and a create with no
timeout waits forever on a host that has wedged.

the runbook now refuses to create a cluster it did not find (CREATE_CLUSTER=1 is the explicit ask,
and CI passes it) and the dev cycle asks before creating one; a command that hangs past its timeout
says which one and stops

### F-452 — The operator planned from the first artifact it ever fetched

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The artifact cache in the operator was keyed by suite and version, and a hit was answered by the
marker file alone: once an archive had been fetched for 1.13.0 the ready marker made every later
fetch for 1.13.0 a no-op, so a rebuilt artifact under an unchanged version never reached the
planning child. The symptom is subtle — the CLI applies a tree carrying the new identity and the
operator reverts it to the old rendering within a minute, while the pods stay healthy on an older
directory that is still whole — so it reads as a generator that ignored the change rather than a
cache that never refreshed. The key now carries the artifact identity, the same name the volume gets
(D-468), so two artifacts of one version are two cache directories and a rebuild is a fetch. The old
directories are left behind: a long-lived operator accumulates one per published artifact, and
nothing prunes them yet (T-286).

Fixed: artifactDir now appends the artifact identity, so the operator's cache is keyed by suite,
version and digest rather than suite and version. Verified end to end — the republished artifact was
fetched into a new cache directory, the child rendered 1.13.0-2f56fe0e with both mounts, and the
reconciled Deployments carry it. Pruning the cache is T-286.

### F-449 — Rush links are absolute, so the fill must run where readers mount

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The k8s intent generates a nodeLocal volume by filling a per-node directory on the host, and Rush's
create-links.js writes _absolute_ links taken from the directory it runs in. A reader that mounted
that directory at /opt/deploy/suite therefore failed its first import with
`Cannot find package '@feasibleone/blong'`: the link carried
`/var/lib/blong/suites/blong-suite/<identity>`, a path the container did not have, and the operator
plus four suite pods crash-looped while kubectl reported nothing worse than
`exceeded its progress deadline`. The diagnosis is cheap once an old volume is inspected directly:
listing its links shows the path they carry. Two shapes were tried before the right one — a second
read-only mount of the node root (D-472, superseded), and mounting the artifact at its own identity
path (D-474, superseded) — and both only arranged for the container to have the path the links
named. The resolution is to remove the coupling: the fill rewrites the links as relative ones, so
the artifact reads from wherever it is mounted (D-476).

### F-456 — The materializer's round trip found three split defects

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

Building the round trip — a materialized base plus overlay against the flat tree — failed before it
passed, and every failure was a defect rather than a test artefact. A patch file is named after the
object's basename, so deployments/access.yaml and services/access.yaml claim the same patch name: a
reader that matches by file name merges a Deployment patch into a Service, which is why the
materializer matches by what a patch targets (apiVersion, kind, namespace, name) the way kustomize
does. The Deployment branch of the split patched every Deployment, so a service's own Deployment —
with no suite volume to replace — got a patch carrying a null volume, and now stays in the base. And
with no digest the artifact identity _is_ the version, so placeholderize destroyed every label that
merely read it while the instance patch put back only two: the patch now carries the object's labels
whole, because a value substitution cannot be undone label by label.

All three defects are fixed in generator.ts and pinned by the round-trip step (84 of 84 realm tests
pass): the instance patch carries the object's labels whole, only a Deployment with a suite volume
is split at all, and the materializer matches patches by target rather than by file name.

### F-457 — A CR pass could not list nodes, so no generation succeeded

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

The operator's install grants cluster-scoped rights in one place, and the node read was not among
them. The plan is made per node — a fill Job for each, over the node-local volume behind it — so a
pass handed a CR whose spec names no nodes has to list them, and every generation answered nodes is
forbidden: no pass could converge on the local dev-cluster, while the CR went on reading Ready,
because the status is only written once the tree materializes. The install now grants get and list
on nodes. The same experiment showed the second half of the trap: CI's wait for the CR phase is
satisfied by a stale Ready, so a job that asserts the phase alone can pass while the operator is
failing.

Fixed. The operator's ClusterRole grants get and list on nodes, the plan is made per node, and the
end-to-end cycle now generates from the shipped base and reaches apply (pass from cr: 5 to create,
16 unchanged, 3 deleted).

### F-458 — The operator read objects in a namespace it held no rights in

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · resolved_

A pass discovers what a suite owns by its labels, so it reads every object that carries them
wherever it sits, while the operator's Role was granted only in the suite's own namespace. The
